newsitem.title: JAPAN: Shipowner says N.Korea corn shipment is from China.
newsitem.headline: Shipowner says N.Korea corn shipment is from China.

text.p: A ship that carried 1,000 tonnes of corn from famine-stricken North Korea to Japan this week was simply transhipping the maize from China in a commercial deal, the operator of the North Korean vessel said on Thursday.

Reports of the shipment had briefly set off a flurry of investigations by Japanese officials and aid organisations mystified at how North Korea was able to export corn when many of its people were near starvation.

"North Korea was only used as a transit port and the corn itself comes from China," said So Chung On, spokesman for the General Association of Korean Residents in Japan, an organisation that represents North Korean interests.
The group operates the ship which carried the cargo.
"It's an obvious act for North Korea to engage in trade activity as it is a way to secure foreign currency," he told Reuters.

A customs spokesman in the northern Japanese port of Aomori said the 3,317-tonne passenger-freighter Mangyongbong '92, the only North Korean ship that regularly sails to Japan, unloaded 1,030 tonnes of maize at the port, 600 km (375 miles) north of Tokyo, on Thursday.
He said the cargo was loaded at the North Korean port of Chongjin on July 12 and arrived at Aomori on Monday.
Japanese government spokesman Kaoru Yosano said the government was investigating the case.
"This is a transaction between private firms but we are investigating the case," Yosano, the deputy chief cabinet secretary, told a news conference.
The Japanese newspaper Sankei Shimbun said a poultry farmer in Yokohama, which adjoins Tokyo, ordered the grain as chicken feed through a Japan-based North Korean trading company.
The newspaper estimated the cargo was worth 13 million yen ($112,000).
The daily said it was the first such export of unprocessed livestock feed from North Korea since 1988.
But an official at the trading company, who refused identify himself, said the maize was from "the northeast region of China".

"Chinese maize exported to Japan is usually loaded from a port in the Dalian region (of China), but using the North Korean port saves a lot of time as well as cutting back costs greatly," the official said.

The customs spokesman said the corn was in "bulk form" and did not come in bags or other containers which could show its origin, particularly if the maize might be connected to international aid relief.

The U.N World Food Programme has said North Korea, hit by two years of devastating floods which have washed away rice paddies, needs more than 1.2 million tonnes of food this year to feed its population.
Members of international aid missions to North Korea have reported that many of the communist nation's people are badly malnourished from the severe food shortages.
They have said that in some areas people were eating grass and tree bark to supplement their meagre diet. ($1=116 yen)
